title: Idols in the Heart; Noah, Daniel, and Job
summary: Elders of Israel come to consult Ezekiel, but God reveals that they have set up idols in their hearts. He will answer such people himself, in judgment, and calls the house of Israel to repent. God then declares that when a land is judged by famine, wild beasts, sword, or plague, even Noah, Daniel, and Job could save only themselves. Jerusalem will face all four, yet a few survivors will reach the exiles, and their lives will show that God did not act without cause.
story: Chapter 13 condemned false prophets. Chapter 14 turns to the other side of the transaction: the people who consult prophets while their real loyalty lies elsewhere. The elders who sit before Ezekiel (verse 1) are the same kind of leaders who sat before him in 8:1 and will again in 20:1. The second half of the chapter takes up a question the exiles must have asked. Surely there were righteous people in Jerusalem, and surely God would spare the city for their sake, as he had been willing to spare Sodom for ten righteous people (Genesis 18:32)? God's answer is that the time for such intercession has passed. The theme of individual responsibility, introduced here, will be developed fully in chapter 18.
historical:
The oracle is undated but fits the years between the deportation of 597 BC and the fall of Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC. The elders of the exile were community leaders who held authority among the deportees in Babylon. Jeremiah's letter to the exiles (Jeremiah 29) shows that the community had its own prophets and leaders and that it remained in contact with Jerusalem.

The three righteous men are a notable trio. Noah and Job are well known from Genesis and the book of Job; both are presented as righteous men who lived outside Israel's covenant history. The identity of Daniel is debated. The Hebrew spelling here is Dan'el, slightly different from the usual spelling of the name of the prophet in the book of Daniel. Some scholars identify him with the Daniel of that book, who according to its own account was taken to Babylon in 605 BC and was known at the royal court for wisdom and faithfulness. Others identify him with Danel, a righteous king and judge in the Aqhat legend from Ugarit, a Canaanite city whose texts date from before 1200 BC, noting that he would pair naturally with Noah and Job as ancient non-Israelite figures. Both views have serious defenders.
cultural:
Consulting a prophet was a normal part of ancient religion. Kings and ordinary people alike went to prophets or diviners for guidance before important decisions, and Israel's kings did so repeatedly (1 Kings 22; 2 Kings 22:13-14). Across the ancient Near East it was assumed that one could approach several gods and several sources of guidance. Ezekiel's elders seem to have done just that: they had not given up the LORD, but they had set up idols in their hearts and wanted a word from his prophet as well.

The idea that a few righteous people could protect a whole community was deeply rooted. Abraham's bargaining over Sodom (Genesis 18) and Moses' intercession for Israel (Exodus 32) show it at work in Israel's own traditions. The four judgments in verse 21 (sword, famine, wild beasts, and plague) are drawn from the covenant curses of Leviticus 26 and appeared together in Ezekiel 5:17. They were the standard catastrophes of the ancient world, the things every farming community feared.
literary: The chapter has two distinct parts. Verses 1 to 11 use the language of Israel's law, with phrases like “any Israelite” and “cut him off from among My people” that echo Leviticus. It is structured as a case: if a person does this, then God will respond in that way. Verses 12 to 23 are also built as a legal case study, with four parallel scenarios (famine, wild beasts, sword, and plague), each ending with the same verdict: even these three men could save only themselves. The repetition drives the point home. The final paragraph (verses 21 to 23) applies the cases to Jerusalem and ends with an unexpected twist: survivors will come, and the exiles will be comforted when they see what kind of people they are.

outline.t: Elders with idols in their hearts
A call to repent and a warning to the inquirer
The deceived prophet and the purpose of judgment
Four judgments, and three righteous men
Jerusalem's survivors and the exiles' consolation

doctrines.note: The chapter locates idolatry in the heart (verse 3). An idol is not only a statue but anything a person sets up as a source of security or guidance in place of God. Such idols make a person estranged from God even while seeking him.

God's command is plain: “Repent and turn away from your idols” (verse 6). The purpose of his response is to “take hold of the hearts” of his people (verse 5) and restore the covenant relationship (verse 11).
The righteousness of a few cannot cover the guilt of a whole people that refuses to turn. Each person stands before God in his own right, a principle that Ezekiel develops in chapter 18.

words.note: Gillulim, idols, Ezekiel's scornful term for false gods. In this chapter they are set up “in their hearts” (verse 3), a striking move from shrines and statues to the inner life. The idol can be present long before there is any image.

Mikhshol, stumbling block, something that causes a person to trip and fall. The elders have placed their own stumbling block before their faces (verses 3, 4, 7). Their idolatry is not just a private matter but something they keep in front of them, shaping everything they see.

Patah, to entice or deceive. Verse 9 says that if a prophet is enticed, it was the LORD who enticed him. The same verb appears in 1 Kings 22, where God allows a lying spirit to entice Ahab's prophets, and in Jeremiah 20:7. It is one of the Old Testament's hard sayings, discussed below.

Tsedaqah, righteousness. It describes right living in line with God's standards and faithful relationship with him. The righteousness of Noah, Daniel, and Job was real, but in this chapter it cannot be transferred to others. It delivers only themselves.

christ: The chapter's claim that even the most righteous human beings can save only themselves sets up one of the central claims of the New Testament. There the righteousness of one man does deliver others: Paul writes that as one trespass led to condemnation for all, so one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all (Romans 5:18-19). The New Testament presents Jesus not as another Noah, Daniel, or Job, whose goodness covered only themselves, but as the righteous one who suffered for the unrighteous to bring them to God (1 Peter 3:18). Ezekiel does not predict this; he shows the limit that only Christ, in the New Testament's account, overcomes.

hard.q: What does it mean that God entices a prophet to speak falsely and then punishes him (verse 9)?
hard.a: This verse troubles many readers. Several responses have been offered. One view reads it in light of 1 Kings 22, where God permits a lying spirit to deceive prophets who already wanted to tell the king what he wished to hear: God gives people over to the deception they have chosen, which becomes itself a judgment. A second view stresses that Hebrew often speaks of God as the cause of everything that happens, including what he permits, without distinguishing primary and secondary causes as later theology does. A third view emphasizes the context: the prophet who gives a comforting word to someone with idols in his heart is already compromised, and God's judgment exposes him. All three agree that the verse does not make God the author of lies in the sense of deceiving the innocent. The text itself ties the prophet's fate to the inquirer's and says the purpose is that Israel would no longer stray (verse 11).

questions: The elders consulted God's prophet while keeping idols in their hearts. What might you be seeking guidance about while holding onto something that competes with God?
Why do you think the chapter insists that even the righteousness of Noah, Daniel, and Job could not save others?
The survivors of Jerusalem would show the exiles that God had not acted without cause. How can seeing the consequences of sin clearly bring a kind of comfort?
